methods.label: Diagonal clearance and a centered rotation
methods.explanation:
The useful length to track is the table's diagonal: it gives both an unavoidable clearance and a way to carry out the move. By the Pythagorean theorem, that length is
\[
d=\sqrt{10^2+8^2}=\sqrt{164}\text{ feet}.
\]
The two positions require the 10-foot sides to change from horizontal to vertical. Track the direction of one such side continuously during the move. It must pass through a quarter-turn clockwise or counterclockwise, even if the motion includes extra turns or backtracking. During a counterclockwise quarter-turn, the diagonal initially slanting downward to the right passes through a horizontal position. During a clockwise quarter-turn, use the diagonal initially slanting upward to the right. Thus, at some point a horizontal diagonal of length \(d\) must fit between the room's vertical walls. Consequently, \(S\ge d\).

To show that this clearance is sufficient, first slide the table to the middle of the room while keeping its sides parallel to the walls. The rectangle fits inside the circle centered at its diagonal intersection and passing through its four corners. This circle has diameter \(d\). When \(S\ge d\), the circle fits inside the square room, so the table can rotate through a quarter-turn about its center without reaching outside the room. Finally, slide it back to the desired corner.

Therefore the exact minimum side length is \(\sqrt{164}\) feet. Since
\[
12^2=144<164<169=13^2,
\]
the smallest integer value is \(\boxed{13}\) feet, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
